events.title: The Fed raises interest rates
events.description: Its short-term target rises to 2.25–2.50% while the economy grows and the job market strengthens.

events.title: The Fed responds to coronavirus disruption
events.description: It cuts its short-term target to 0–0.25% and announces support for borrowing and financial markets.

events.title: Microsoft reports stronger cloud demand
events.description: Services delivered over the internet bring in more revenue as remote work grows. Advertising and some other sales are weaker.

events.title: Apple splits each share into four
events.description: Owners receive four shares for each one they held. The split alone does not make their investment worth more.

events.title: ExxonMobil reports a large annual loss
events.description: The company reports losing $22.4 billion in 2020, including reductions in the recorded value of assets, amid difficult energy markets.

what_happened_next.text:
The five years after February 2016 brought changing interest rates and business conditions. In December 2018, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates. In March 2020, the coronavirus outbreak disrupted daily life and business. The Fed quickly cut rates close to zero and took steps to help markets and lending.

Microsoft said that working and learning from home increased demand for its cloud services—online tools for storing and working with information. Some online ads and software purchases weakened. Microsoft reported that its cloud business brought in more than $50 billion a year.

Apple reported $59.7 billion in revenue—money from sales—in the quarter ending June 2020, 11% more than a year earlier. It also said each share would split into four. Owners would have four shares where they had one, but their total investment would not become four times as valuable just from the split. Exxon Mobil reported a $22.4 billion loss for 2020 during a difficult year for energy companies.

The game ends in February 2021. No one starting in 2016 knew when a pandemic would arrive or how these companies would change.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: In 2016, Apple talked about its devices, Microsoft about its cloud services—online tools for storing information and using software—and Exxon Mobil about weak oil prices. The starting news also included community, health, science, and entertainment stories.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: Over the next five years, the economy and the three companies changed in different ways. The pandemic changed how people lived and worked. No single headline tells the whole story of what happened to these investments.
reflection.what_faded_away: Football season and award shows passed, and new stories took their place. Those headlines were part of the day, but they could not tell people what would happen to the companies over five years.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: In February 2016, no one knew when a new coronavirus would spread around the world or how much it would change daily life and businesses. Nobody knew the emergency steps the Fed would take or how each company would respond.
